facts.fact: The Indian Constitution is the lengthiest written constitution in the world.
Constitutions are classified as written (like the USA) or unwritten (like the UK).
Originally the Constitution had a Preamble, 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.
The source counts 448 Articles in 25 Parts and 12 Schedules (October 2024).
The Constitution has been amended 106 times as of 2024.
Its length is due to diversity, the 1935 Act, a single constitution for Centre and states, and legal experts.
Borrowed features were adapted: the cabinet system does not have the same supremacy as in the UK.
The Constitution is a blend of rigidity and flexibility.
Article 368 provides for amendment by special majority and by special majority with ratification by half the states.
A special majority is a majority of the total membership of each House plus two-thirds of members present and voting.
Some provisions can be amended by a simple majority — more than half of those present and voting — by the ordinary legislative process.
Federal features: two governments, division of powers, written and supreme constitution, rigidity, independent judiciary and bicameralism.
Unitary features: strong Centre, single constitution, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, Centre-appointed Governors, all-India services, emergency provisions.
K.C. Wheare described India as 'quasi-federal'.
Article 1 describes India as a 'Union of States'.
The Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the states.
No state has the right to secede from the Indian Union.
The word 'Federation' is not used anywhere in the Constitution.
Granville Austin called Indian federalism 'co-operative federalism'.
Morris-Jones called it 'bargaining federalism'.
Ivor Jennings called India a federation with a strong centralising tendency.
The parliamentary system is also called the Westminster model, responsible government and cabinet government.
India chose the British parliamentary system over the American presidential system, at the Centre and in the states.
Parliamentary features include nominal and real executives, majority-party rule, collective responsibility and dissolution of the lower House.
Unlike the British Parliament, the Indian Parliament is not sovereign.
Unlike Britain's hereditary monarch, India has an elected head of State.
In a parliamentary system the Government is responsible to Parliament and can be removed by it.
The Constitution synthesises British parliamentary sovereignty and American judicial supremacy.
Article 21 uses 'procedure established by law', not the American 'due process of law'.
The Supreme Court can strike down laws by judicial review, while Parliament can amend most of the Constitution.
A single integrated judiciary, headed by the Supreme Court, enforces both central and state laws.
The Supreme Court is a federal court, the highest court of appeal, guarantor of FRs and guardian of the Constitution.
Judicial independence is secured by security of tenure and fixed service conditions.
The Election Commission, CAG, UPSC and State PSCs are independent constitutional bodies.
NITI Aayog is not a constitutional body; it was created by a Cabinet resolution in 2015.
The CAG audits the accounts of the central and state governments.
The UPSC advises the President and a State PSC advises the Governor on disciplinary matters.
A National Emergency (Article 352) can be declared on war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
President's Rule rests on Article 356, and on Article 365 when a state fails to comply with Union directions.
A Financial Emergency (Article 360) can be proclaimed on a threat to financial stability or credit.
'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Indian secularism is positive — equal respect and protection for all religions — unlike the Western separation of religion and state.
Universal adult franchise is in Article 326.
The 61st Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 (in force 1989).
Despite a dual polity India has a single citizenship, unlike the dual citizenship of the USA.
India has only one citizenship and one domicile (UPSC 2021).
The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) created a third tier of local government.
The 73rd Amendment added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule for panchayats.
The 74th Amendment added Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule for municipalities.
Lokanath Misra called the Constitution a 'slavish imitation of the West'.
K. Hanumanthaiya complained of an English band instead of the music of the veena or sitar (un-Gandhian criticism).
Ivor Jennings called the Constitution a 'paradise for lawyers'.
Criticisms include: borrowed, carbon copy of the 1935 Act, un-Indian, un-Gandhian, elephantine size and lawyers' paradise.
A constitutional government restricts State authority in the interest of individual liberty.
Separation of powers is the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy (UPSC 2021).
Part III guarantees six Fundamental Rights.
The Right to Equality is in Articles 14-18 and abolishes untouchability.
The Right to Freedom is in Articles 19-22, including protection against arbitrary arrest and detention.
The Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24) bans trafficking, forced labour and child labour.
The Right to Freedom of Religion is in Articles 25-28.
Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30) protect minorities' language, script and culture.
Article 32 gives the Right to Constitutional Remedies — moving the Supreme Court.
Writs are derived from the legal system of England and enforced through Article 32.
Habeas Corpus means 'you may have the body' — to produce a detained person before a court.
Mandamus means 'we command' — directs an official to perform a public duty.
Prohibition is issued by a higher court to stop a lower court exceeding its jurisdiction.
Certiorari quashes an order of a lower court made without jurisdiction or against natural justice.
Quo Warranto means 'by what authority' — questions the right to hold a public office.
Part IVA has only Article 51A, listing eleven Fundamental Duties.
The Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, during the internal Emergency.
The 86th Amendment (2002) added one more Fundamental Duty.
Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable.
Ambedkar called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Constitution.
The Directive Principles fall into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groups.
Directive Principles are non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
The ideal of a 'Welfare State' is enshrined in the Directive Principles.
'Economic Justice' is provided in both the Preamble and the Directive Principles.
UDHR (1948) ideals are reflected in the Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties.
'To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India' is a Fundamental Duty (Article 51A).
The 97th Amendment (2011) gave constitutional status to co-operative societies.
The right to form co-operative societies is a Fundamental Right under Article 19.
The 97th Amendment added Article 43B, a Directive Principle on promoting co-operative societies.
The 97th Amendment added Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT) on co-operative societies.
The Preamble is the introductory statement setting out the guiding principles and philosophy of the Constitution.
The Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru.
The Preamble has four components: source of authority, nature of the State, objectives and date of adoption.
'We, the people of India' shows that the Constitution derives its authority from the people.
The Preamble describes India as Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic and Republic.
The four objectives are Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
The Preamble records the date of adoption as 26 November 1949.
Justice in the Preamble is social, economic and political.
Liberty in the Preamble is of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
'Economic liberty' is not an objective in the Preamble.
Equality in the Preamble is of status and of opportunity.
Fraternity assures the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation.
The Preamble ends 'do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution'.
Sovereign means India is independent, with no external authority above it.
Socialist in India means democratic socialism — a mixed economy.
Democratic means representative parliamentary democracy.
Republic means the head of State is elected, not hereditary.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble.
The Preamble has been amended only once.
On 26 January 1950 India was a Sovereign Democratic Republic.
In November 2024 (Dr Balram Singh v. Union of India) the Supreme Court upheld the insertion of Socialist and Secular.
In S.R. Bommai (1994) secularism was held part of the basic structure.
Berubari (1960): the Preamble is the 'key to open the mind of the makers' but not a part of the Constitution.
The Berubari case was a Presidential reference under Article 143.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): the Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable, but not its basic features.
LIC of India (1995): the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution but not directly enforceable.
The Preamble is part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts (UPSC 2020).
The Preamble is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a limitation on it.
The mind of the makers of the Constitution is reflected in the Preamble (UPSC 2017).
'We, the people of India' (the idea of a Preamble) comes from the USA.
The ideal of social, economic and political justice comes from the Russian Revolution.
Liberty, equality and fraternity come from the French Revolution.
Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar said the Preamble 'expresses what we had thought or dreamt for so long'.
K.M. Munshi called the Preamble the 'horoscope' of our sovereign democratic republic.
Thakur Das Bhargava called the Preamble the 'soul' of the Constitution and 'a jewel set in it'.
Ernest Barker called the Preamble the 'key-note' to the Constitution.
M. Hidayatullah compared the Preamble to the American Declaration of Independence.
N.A. Palkhivala called the Preamble the 'identity card' of the Constitution.

Part II deals with Citizenship (Articles 5-11).
Part III deals with Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35).
Part IV deals with Directive Principles (Articles 36-51).
Part IVA deals with Fundamental Duties (Articles 51A).
Part V deals with The Union (Articles 52-151).
Part VI deals with The States (Articles 152-237).
Part VIII deals with Union Territories (Articles 239-242).
Part IX deals with Panchayats (Articles 243-243O).
Part IXA deals with Municipalities (Articles 243P-243ZG).
Part X deals with Scheduled and Tribal Areas (Articles 244-244A).
Part XI deals with Relations between the Union and the States (Articles 245-263).

facts.fact: Part XII deals with Finance, Property, Contracts (Articles 264-300A).
Part XIII deals with Trade (Articles 301-307).
Part XIV deals with Services (Articles 308-323).
Part XIVA deals with Tribunals (Articles 323A-323B).
Part XV deals with Elections (Articles 324-329A).
Part XVI deals with Special provisions (Articles 330-342).
Part XVII deals with Official Language (Articles 343-351).
Part XVIII deals with Emergency Provisions (Articles 352-360).
Part XIX deals with Miscellaneous (Articles 361-367).
Part XX deals with Amendment of the Constitution (Articles 368).
Part XXI deals with Temporary, Transitional and Special (Articles 369-392).
Part XXII deals with Short title (Articles 393-395).
There are now 25 Parts; IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA were added later.
Part VII (Part B states) was repealed by the 7th Amendment (1956).
Part XIII on trade and commerce is inspired by the Australian Constitution.
Part III (Fundamental Rights) was inspired by the US Bill of Rights.
Within Part V: Union Executive 52-78, Parliament 79-122, Supreme Court 124-147.
Within Part VI: State Executive 153-167, Legislature 168-212, High Courts 214-237.
Legislative relations are Articles 245-255 and administrative relations 256-263.
The original Constitution was handwritten in both Hindi and English.
Article 371D (32nd Amendment, 1973) gives Andhra Pradesh equitable opportunities in public employment and education.
After 2014 Article 371D applies to both Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
Article 371E lets Parliament provide for a Central University in Andhra Pradesh.
The First Schedule deals with States and Union Territories (Articles 1 and 4).
The First Schedule is linked to Article(s) 1 and 4.
The Second Schedule deals with Salaries (Articles 59).
The Second Schedule is linked to Article(s) 59.
The Third Schedule deals with oaths (Articles 75).
The Third Schedule is linked to Article(s) 75.
The Fourth Schedule deals with Rajya Sabha (Articles 80).
The Fourth Schedule is linked to Article(s) 80.
The Fifth Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas (Articles 244(1)).
The Fifth Schedule is linked to Article(s) 244(1).
The Sixth Schedule deals with Tribal Areas (Articles 244(2)).
The Sixth Schedule is linked to Article(s) 244(2).
The Seventh Schedule deals with Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Articles 246).
The Seventh Schedule is linked to Article(s) 246.
The Eighth Schedule deals with 22 (Articles 344 and 351).
The Eighth Schedule is linked to Article(s) 344 and 351.
The Ninth Schedule deals with land reform (Articles 31B).
The Ninth Schedule is linked to Article(s) 31B.
The Tenth Schedule deals with Anti-defection (Articles 102 and 191).
The Tenth Schedule is linked to Article(s) 102 and 191.
The Eleventh Schedule deals with Panchayats (Articles 243G).
The Eleventh Schedule is linked to Article(s) 243G.
The Twelfth Schedule deals with Municipalities (Articles 243W).
The Twelfth Schedule is linked to Article(s) 243W.
Schedules were first used in the GoI Act 1935, which had 10 Schedules.
Schedules hold detail outside the main text and make amendment easier.
The Ninth Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment Act, 1951.
The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985.
The Eleventh Schedule came with the 73rd and the Twelfth with the 74th Amendment (1992).
The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for Panchayats.
The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects for Municipalities.
The Eighth Schedule originally had 14 languages; it now has 22.
In I.R. Coelho (2007) laws put in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 were held open to basic-structure review.
From Britain: parliamentary government, rule of law, bicameralism, cabinet system, single citizenship, writs.
From the USA: FRs, independence of judiciary, judicial review, impeachment of President, removal of judges, Vice-President.
From Ireland: DPSP, method of President's election, nomination of Rajya Sabha members.
From the USSR: Fundamental Duties and the ideal of justice in the Preamble.
From Canada: strong-centre federation, residuary powers, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of SC.
From Australia: Concurrent List, joint sitting, freedom of trade and commerce.
From Weimar Germany: suspension of FRs during emergency.
From France: republic and ideals of liberty, equality, fraternity.
From Japan: procedure established by law.
From the GoI Act 1935: federal scheme, judiciary, PSCs, office of Governor, emergency provisions.
From South Africa: amendment procedure and election of Rajya Sabha members.
